interview_metadata.name: Mary Alberti
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Okay, sure. So I'm Mary, I'm 28, and I've been in Madison my whole life. I grew up over on the west side, in a little Italian-American household — my grandparents came over from Bari in the sixties, and my dad Frank runs a small HVAC business, my mom Teresa worked the front desk at a dentist's office for about twenty years. We were Catholic, went to St. Maria Goretti for Mass, Sunday dinners at Nonna's with homemade tagliatelle and gravy — real red gravy, not pasta sauce. That's a big deal in my family. I did public school, Memorial High, graduated in 2015. I wasn't a bad student but I was never gonna be the college kid — my brother Anthony, he's the one who went to UW-Whitewater for business. I started at a Culver's right after graduation, moved to a different counter job, and I've been at my current spot — I work front counter at a quick-service place near the west side — for about four and a half years now. Big life stuff? My grandma passed in 2022, that wrecked me for a while. I broke up with a boyfriend of almost three years right before the pandemic, his name was Kyle, and honestly that kind of reset my whole trajectory — I got really into bullet journaling, started running around Lake Mendota, joined the Madison Runners Club. I save money now like it's a religion. I'm trying to get promoted to shift supervisor this year, and the long game is I want to open a little diner someday. That's the story, more or less.

follow_ups.question: You mentioned Nonna's Sunday dinners — is that tradition still going?
follow_ups.response: Not really, not since Nonna died in '22. My mom tries to host once a month but it's never the same. She does the bracciole, but it's not Nonna's hand on the rolling pin, you know? I still make the tagliatelle from scratch maybe once every couple months, usually for myself on a Sunday off.

follow_ups.question: What was it about the breakup with Kyle that reset things?
follow_ups.response: We'd been saving for a duplex together and when it ended I realized I'd been planning my whole life around his timeline. So I reset. I started keeping a bullet journal — like an actual Leuchtturm1917 with the dot grid, full Ryder Carroll method — and I just started tracking everything. Spending, running mileage, shifts. It sounds obsessive but it's how I got back on my feet.

follow_ups.question: Is opening a diner a serious plan or more of a dream?
follow_ups.response: Serious. I've got a tab in my journal labeled 'Diner' with a savings target — I'm not gonna say the number — and I'm signed up to start the hospitality management associate's at Madison College in the fall, part-time. ServSafe Manager cert is on the list for this year too.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: Yeah, definitely. Spring of 2020 — right when everything shut down — Kyle and I broke up, and at the same time my store was bleeding employees. My GM at the time, Denise, pulled me aside and said she could either keep me as a crew member part-time, or I could step up, take extra shifts, learn the opening routine, and basically become the person who held the place together. I had to decide in like a week. One path was moving back in with my parents and maybe going back to school for nursing, which my mom wanted. The other was doubling down on food service, which everybody in my family thought was temporary. I took Denise's offer. I learned the opening, I learned inventory, I learned the POS backend. That's when I stopped thinking of this as a job I was killing time at and started thinking of it as a career I could actually own.

follow_ups.question: Did your family push back on that choice?
follow_ups.response: Oh yeah. My mom still brings up nursing at Thanksgiving. My dad's more supportive — he started his HVAC business from a van, so he gets the 'work your way up' thing.

follow_ups.question: Is Denise still around?
follow_ups.response: She transferred to a store in Sun Prairie about a year ago but we still text. She's one of my references for the supervisor promotion.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I remember writing the pros and cons out in my journal on a Tuesday night with a glass of New Glarus Spotted Cow next to me. I'm not a 'just happened' person — I overthink everything.

follow_ups.question: Do you still have that journal entry?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I keep all my old journals in a plastic bin under my bed. That one's labeled 'Q2 2020.'

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Honestly Denise was that person. I didn't need a lot else. Maybe if there'd been a better resource at Madison College for working adults — a clearer path to the hospitality program — I would've enrolled three years sooner.

follow_ups.question: What would've made the college path easier?
follow_ups.response: Evening advising. I can't take a Tuesday at 2pm off work to meet with an advisor. Everything's built for 22-year-olds.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: No partner right now, no kids. I've been single about a year and change — I dated a guy named Ben, a carpenter, for eight months last year, ended it amicably. Family-wise, my parents Frank and Teresa still live in the house I grew up in on the west side, maybe fifteen minutes from my apartment. My brother Anthony's 31, lives in Milwaukee with his wife Jenna and their two kids — Luca who's four and Sofia who's almost two. I see them maybe once a month; I drive up Saturday morning and come back Sunday. My aunt Rosa — my dad's sister — lives in Fitchburg and I see her more often, usually Sunday dinners at my parents'. Nonna passed but my grandpa Joe is still around, he's 84, in an assisted living place in Middleton. I visit him every other Sunday for about an hour and a half, bring him a biscotti and we watch the Packers or the Brewers depending on season. Family is the center of a lot of my week, actually.

follow_ups.question: How often do you talk to your parents?
follow_ups.response: Phone call with my mom every other day, basically. Dad I see in person on Sundays. Mom's a texter, she sends me recipes and Marketplace listings for furniture.

follow_ups.question: What about Anthony?
follow_ups.response: We group-text a lot — him, me, and Jenna. Mostly about the kids or Packers games. He's the planner in the family, I'm the one who actually shows up.

follow_ups.question: Any plans for kids yourself?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, eventually. I want one or two, but not till I'm in a stable partnership and the diner thing is more than a spreadsheet. I'm in no rush — 32, 33 maybe.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My cousin Gianna — Rosa's daughter — she's 26, we're close, she works at a dental lab. We do brunch once a month.

follow_ups.question: Where do you two usually go for brunch?
follow_ups.response: Marigold Kitchen downtown, or Short Stack Eatery if the wait's not insane.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: Yeah, I've got a pretty tight friend group. My best friend is Lauren — we've been friends since ninth grade at Memorial. She's a dental hygienist, married, no kids yet. We talk daily. Then there's my running crew — Becca, Priya, and Danielle from the Madison Runners Club. We do Saturday long runs and brunch after. And there's a small crew from work I'd call actual friends — Marcus who does line, and Jess who's another counter worker. I'd say I have maybe six people I'd call at 2am if something went wrong.

follow_ups.question: How did you meet the running crew?
follow_ups.response: Joined the club in summer 2021 after the breakup. Becca showed up in the same trail shoes as me and we just clicked on mile three around Picnic Point.

follow_ups.question: Do you see Lauren weekly?
follow_ups.response: At least. Usually Wednesday night wine at her place, or she comes to mine. We also do a standing pedicure every six weeks.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in a one-bedroom apartment in the 53717 zip code, out by High Point Road on the west side. It's a mix of apartment complexes, a few single-family neighborhoods, a big church, and a lot of chain stores — Target, Woodman's, Trader Joe's. It's quiet. Lots of families, lots of people walking dogs. It's not the cool Willy Street scene, but I can get on the Beltline in five minutes and I'm ten minutes from my parents. The running is decent — I mostly drive over to Lake Mendota for the real runs but I can do a three-miler on the neighborhood sidewalks if I'm short on time. Rent's reasonable by Madison standards — I pay $1,185 for the one-bedroom, which is not a steal but it's not $1,600 like closer in.

follow_ups.question: How long have you been in this apartment?
follow_ups.response: Three years this June. Signed the lease right after I moved out of Kyle's place.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: The couple across the hall, John and Mei, yeah — we trade packages. Everyone else I nod to. It's friendly-ish but not tight.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe. I run at 5:30 in the morning sometimes and I've never felt uncomfortable. There was a car break-in in the lot last fall but that's it.

follow_ups.question: Did they break into your car?
follow_ups.response: No, a neighbor's. They got a Garmin and some change. I started putting my stuff in the trunk after that.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: Up: quiet, close to family, easy to drive. Down: it's a little isolating, not a lot of walkable stuff. If I want to meet a friend for a drink I have to drive or Uber. I miss living closer to the isthmus sometimes.

follow_ups.question: Would you move if you could?
follow_ups.response: Eventually, maybe Schenk-Atwood or Tenney-Lapham when I can afford it. But for saving purposes, I'm staying put.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It's just me. I live alone in the one-bedroom. No roommates, no partner, no pets — well, I want a cat, I've been on a shelter waitlist at Dane County Humane for a tabby, but I haven't pulled the trigger. So, household of one.

follow_ups.question: Why hesitate on the cat?
follow_ups.response: Vet bills and the shift schedule. I'm gone ten-hour days sometimes. I want to wait till I'm supervisor and my hours are more consistent.

follow_ups.question: Do you like living alone?
follow_ups.response: Love it. I've got my routines, nobody touches my coffee setup, I can bullet journal at the kitchen table at 10pm in silence.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Just me, permanent.

follow_ups.question: No visitors staying over right now?
follow_ups.response: Nope.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: My cousin Gianna crashes on the couch maybe twice a year when she's in from a work trip. That's it.

follow_ups.question: Anyone else overnight occasionally?
follow_ups.response: Lauren, maybe once every few months after too much wine. Nothing regular.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody.

follow_ups.question: Just confirming — no one out of town who normally lives here?
follow_ups.response: Nope, just me.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My weeks are pretty structured. I work five days, usually a mix of openers and mid-shifts. Opener days — Monday, Wednesday, Friday most weeks — I'm up at 4:15, at the store by 5:15, we open at 6. Shift ends around 2pm. Mid-shifts I'm there 10am to 7pm. I run three days a week — Tuesday and Thursday mornings before a mid-shift, long run Saturday with the club. Sundays are family. I journal every night for like fifteen minutes, meal-prep Sundays, grocery run Sunday afternoon at Woodman's. Wednesday nights are Lauren wine nights. Thursday I usually do Sudoku and read for an hour before bed.

follow_ups.question: What time do you go to bed on opener nights?
follow_ups.response: 9pm, lights out by 9:15. I'm militant about it.

follow_ups.question: Do you take a full day off?
follow_ups.response: Usually Sunday's my real off day. I'll still prep and do errands but no shift.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: One job. I'm a counter worker at a quick-service restaurant on the west side — I'd rather not say the chain specifically, but think Midwestern fast-casual, burgers and frozen custard. I handle POS, cash, customer issues, some light inventory, and I've been training the new hires for about a year. Scheduled 38-40 hours a week, five days, mix of openers and mids as I said. Occasional Saturday if somebody calls out.

follow_ups.question: What's your hourly rate, if you don't mind sharing?
follow_ups.response: $16.50 an hour right now. Supervisor would bump me to about $19.75 plus a small monthly bonus tied to store metrics.

follow_ups.question: Do you pick up overtime?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, maybe four extra hours a month. My GM tries to cap OT for labor cost but she'll give it to me first because I actually show up.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: Let me think. I tend a raised-bed garden in the shared plot behind my building — tomatoes, green beans, basil, a little rosemary. That's a Saturday afternoon thing April through October. I visit Grandpa Joe every other Sunday. I'm the unofficial IT person for my parents, which means a FaceTime every Sunday about their Wi-Fi or their iPad. And I do a monthly budget review, last Saturday of the month, I sit down with my journal and my bank statements and reconcile everything.

follow_ups.question: How big is the garden plot?
follow_ups.response: Maybe 4 by 8 feet. Enough for me and to give a bag of tomatoes to my mom every week in August.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Big one: I started training new hires in January, so my mid-shifts now have an extra layer of responsibility. I also started a twice-weekly strength training thing at Anytime Fitness — Tuesday and Thursday afternoons between shifts and runs — because my runs had plateaued. And I just registered for my first fall class at Madison College, so I'll be blocking out Monday evenings for homework starting August.

follow_ups.question: How's the training-new-hires piece going?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Some kids pick up the POS in an afternoon, some need a week. It's teaching me patience, which is not my strength.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have kids, so no routine to describe there. My nephew Luca's in preschool three days a week and my niece Sofia is home with Jenna, but that's not my household.

follow_ups.question: Do you do any childcare for them?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally. I'll take Luca for a Saturday afternoon when I'm up in Milwaukee — we go to the zoo or the children's museum.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: Pretty minimal. I got pulled over once in 2019 for a busted taillight in Middleton, officer was nice, gave me a warning. We get cops in the restaurant at shift change sometimes — I know a couple of them by first name. That's really it for direct contact.

follow_ups.question: Any negative experiences?
follow_ups.response: Not personally, no.

follow_ups.question: How about family members?
follow_ups.response: My brother Anthony got a DUI in college, 2014. He did the diversion program, it's expunged now. Nobody else.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: We had a guy get belligerent in the drive-thru last year, threw a drink at Jess. We called MPD, two officers came, they handled it fine. That's pretty much the highlight reel.

follow_ups.question: How did Jess handle it?
follow_ups.response: She was rattled. We let her take a long break. Now we have a stronger de-escalation script.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: Just my brother's DUI back in 2014. Nobody else has been arrested that I know of. I've never been arrested.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect how your family views law enforcement?
follow_ups.response: My dad was angry at Anthony, not at the cops. He thinks Anthony deserved it. Honestly I agree.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote every presidential and every midterm. I skipped the last spring primary for state supreme court, which I feel bad about — I was working an opener that day. I vote in Dane County, in person usually, but I've done absentee a couple times.

follow_ups.question: Do you research candidates?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, I read the Wisconsin State Journal endorsement summaries and I look at Ballotpedia for down-ballot. Nothing deep, but I don't just show up blind.

follow_ups.question: Any local races you've paid attention to?
follow_ups.response: The Madison mayor race and our alderperson race. I don't always know the school board people, which is a gap.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I'd say I'm a moderate Democrat, kind of pragmatic. My family's split — my dad's a Reagan-era Republican, votes Republican but he's not MAGA, he's more like old-school Chamber of Commerce. My mom votes Democrat. I came out of the house in the middle and Madison pushed me left. I'm pro-labor — I think fast food workers deserve more, I think unions are a good thing, I think healthcare should be less of a nightmare. I'm pretty strongly pro-choice. On guns I'm kind of in the middle — my dad hunts, I grew up around rifles in a locked cabinet, but I think background checks are obvious and I don't get the AR-15 thing. I'm fiscally cautious personally — I don't love deficit spending but I also think we underinvest in schools and infrastructure. On immigration I'm pro, my grandparents were immigrants. On police, I think they should exist and be better trained and more accountable. Where I probably diverge from a lot of Madison progressives is I don't love a lot of the really-online lefty stuff — I think there's a performative element that turns me off. I'm practical. I want things to actually work.

follow_ups.question: Who did you vote for in the last presidential?
follow_ups.response: I voted for the Democratic candidate. Both times. But not with enormous enthusiasm.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics at work?
follow_ups.response: Basically never. It's a mixed crew politically and it's just not worth the fight on a Tuesday lunch rush.

follow_ups.question: Any Republicans in your close circle?
follow_ups.response: My dad. A couple coworkers, Marcus the line cook actually leans right. We've had good conversations. I don't think most people are as far apart as the news makes it seem.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've gotten more pro-labor in the last three years. Watching my store run short-staffed for months, watching people burn out, watching what a fifty-cent raise does to turnover — it's made me more sympathetic to the idea that workers need real leverage. I've also gotten more skeptical of both parties on healthcare. My grandpa's assisted living bills are insane and neither party is serious about it, in my opinion. I've gotten a little less patient with social media politics, more interested in local stuff. I donated $40 to our alderperson's campaign last fall, which is the first political donation I've ever made.

follow_ups.question: Anything that moved you rightward?
follow_ups.response: Public safety stuff, maybe a little. When there were issues on State Street last summer I was less 'defund' and more 'let's fund training and mental health response together.'

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: Somewhat, I'd say. 2020 was a big year for me thinking about this stuff — the George Floyd thing, the marches on Capitol Square, all of it. I didn't march but I watched a lot and I read. Being a white woman in a pretty white city, I had to do some of my own homework. It didn't change my life the way it changed a lot of Black folks' lives, and I want to be honest about that.

follow_ups.question: What did the homework look like?
follow_ups.response: I read 'Between the World and Me' by Coates, some Ibram X. Kendi. I listened to a lot of NPR Code Switch. I'm not claiming I'm an expert.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you interact with customers or coworkers?
follow_ups.response: I think I got more thoughtful about who gets the benefit of the doubt in a dispute at the counter. It's a small thing but it matters on a shift.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issues — police accountability, racial disparities in who gets stopped and who gets charged — are real, and I support reforms. I'm less convinced by some of the bigger systemic rebuild arguments, not because I disagree entirely but because I don't trust the people who would be in charge of rebuilding. I think local stuff, like our police oversight board in Madison, is where actual progress happens. I also think the backlash has been worse than the moment itself, and that worries me.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel like the conversation has changed since 2020?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, it's colder now. Less energy, less listening. I think that's a loss.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: It's heavy. I think we've regressed a little in the last few years, or at least the conversation has. I see it in customers sometimes — the edge in how someone will speak to a Black coworker versus me. I think Madison is in a bubble, and I try to remember that when I read the news. I also think class is tangled up in all of this in a way that a lot of political talk misses. A lot of working-class people of every race are struggling, and pitting them against each other is just useful for somebody in power.

follow_ups.question: Have you had direct conversations about race at work?
follow_ups.response: A few. My coworker Desiree and I had a long talk after the Tyre Nichols stuff. Mostly I listen.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Talked to family and friends. Didn't march. Donated once to the Freedom Inc. local group in Madison, small amount. Mostly a listener and a reader, not a loud voice.

follow_ups.question: Any specific family conversation stand out?
follow_ups.response: My dad and I had a tough one in 2020 that ended okay. We agreed more than we thought we would.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: Lauren was pretty engaged in 2020, marched a couple times, she's more vocal on Instagram than me. My running friend Priya, who's South Asian, thinks a lot of the white-liberal stuff is performative and she's been vocal about that. Becca is quieter, similar to me. My brother Anthony is skeptical of a lot of it and we've had some tense group chats.

follow_ups.question: Has it strained any relationships?
follow_ups.response: Not broken any, but definitely some cooler moments with Anthony for a while.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Generally good. I'm 28, 5'6", about 145 pounds, I run 15-20 miles a week, I sleep well on a normal shift schedule. I've got mild seasonal allergies — Zyrtec from April through June. I had plantar fasciitis in 2023 which I rehabbed. I've got a mild GERD thing that flares if I drink too much coffee or beer. I'm on the pill for birth control. That's the picture.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, Dr. Kaufman at Group Health Cooperative. Annual physical in January, dermatology once a year.

follow_ups.question: Any mental health stuff worth naming?
follow_ups.response: I had mild depression after the breakup and after Nonna died. Saw a therapist through EAP for six sessions in 2022. Not currently in therapy.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy: I like routines, so exercise and sleep aren't hard to maintain. I cook at home. I have a decent insurance plan through work, GHC, small copays. Hard: shift work. Opening at 5:15 means I can't always get enough sleep on back-to-back opener nights. And I work around fried food all day, so willpower matters.

follow_ups.question: Do you eat the food at work?
follow_ups.response: A little. I get one free meal per shift, I usually do the grilled chicken sandwich and a small custard on Fridays.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Plantar fasciitis in the summer of 2023 was the big one. I had to stop running for three months, did PT twice a week at UW Health Rehab, got new running shoes — Brooks Glycerin now — and custom insoles. Fully resolved. Otherwise the GERD diagnosis in 2024, which is managed with omeprazole occasionally and watching my coffee intake. Nothing else.

follow_ups.question: Was the PT expensive?
follow_ups.response: Copay was $30 a visit, so about $240 total. Not a disaster.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: The plantar fasciitis didn't stop work — I was on my feet every shift, which is part of why it took so long to heal. No kids to care for. No real work disruption.

follow_ups.question: Did you get any accommodations at work?
follow_ups.response: I switched to cushioned mats behind the counter and my GM let me take more POS shifts, less kitchen, during the worst of it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yeah, two things. Nonna had vascular dementia the last three years of her life and that was hard on all of us, especially Mom. She passed in October 2022. And my grandpa Joe has a heart condition — afib, managed with meds — and he's in assisted living, so I visit and help coordinate stuff with my parents. My mom had a benign breast lump scare in 2023 that turned out fine but was a rough month.

follow_ups.question: Did Nonna's dementia affect your day-to-day a lot?
follow_ups.response: The last six months, yeah. I was spending a weekend a month helping my mom at Nonna's house. It was a second job emotionally.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I've been lucky — GHC is a good HMO, I've never forgone care for myself. The only thing is I put off a dental crown in 2023 for about six months because my dental benefits at work are bad. Eventually I paid out of pocket, about $1,100. Beyond that, it's been okay.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents have good coverage?
follow_ups.response: Dad's self-employed, so they're on an ACA plan. It's okay but the deductibles hurt them.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: A little. My aunt Rosa is into herbal teas, acupuncture, that kind of thing. I've done acupuncture twice for the plantar fasciitis — not sure it helped but didn't hurt. My mom does a lot of what I'd call Italian grandma medicine — hot water with lemon, garlic for colds, ginger compresses. Nothing really fringe.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any supplements?
follow_ups.response: Vitamin D in winter, magnesium at night, a multivitamin. That's it.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I drink, not heavily. I like craft beer — Spotted Cow, Ale Asylum, anything at a Wisconsin brewery. I'd say four to six beers a week, usually Friday and Saturday, sometimes a Wednesday wine with Lauren. During the breakup in 2020 I drank more — probably closer to ten a week for a few months. I pulled back. I don't smoke cigarettes, never have. Occasional edible maybe three times a year, nothing regular.

follow_ups.question: Any concern about the drinking?
follow_ups.response: Not currently. I track it in my journal loosely and I know what my line is. The 2020 stretch scared me a bit.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: Prescriptions, just the birth control pill and occasional omeprazole. No opioids ever — they didn't even prescribe me anything for the plantar fasciitis, just ibuprofen.
